- Environments: production + staging + a small dev sandbox (we discussed ~3 total envs).

2) A nominal target price per 1M tokens to use internally for budget planning.
3) Confirmation of which environments should be licensed / metered.

Subject: Re: On-prem pricing & environment sizing — follow-up and numbers

Alex — great questions. I answered inline and attached a simple model (acme_onprem_pricing_v1.xlsx) so you can tweak token volumes. Short answers first, then the model assumptions below.

1) Reserved capacity meaning
- Two common approaches we offer for on-prem/VPC:
  a) Reserved GPU nodes (capacity-based license): customer purchases N reserved nodes (or vGPU equivalents) for a term. This yields predictable monthly capacity and a lower per-token rate for committed throughput. Overages are billed per 1M tokens at a nominal overage rate.
  b) Committed token throughput (usage-based commit): customer commits to X tokens/month in exchange for a blended $/1M-token price; if you exceed commit, overage rates apply. This is simpler when traffic is bursty and you want price predictability versus node management.

2) Environment licensing
- Typical setup: production + staging are licensed (either covered by the capacity pool or by separate entitlements). Dev sandbox often left unmetered or included as a non-prod entitlement with limited performance. For your case, I recommend: Prod (licensed), Staging (licensed, smaller entitlement), Dev (sandbox - non-metered).

3) Metering model
- We can do a pooled token model across environments (preferred) so you don't get double-billed for cross-env testing. Invoicing shows aggregated committed vs usage and itemized by environment if you want visibility.

Pricing ballpark (12-month term commit) — using your 20M–50M tokens/month, and assuming mixed traffic profile:
- Option A: Reserved nodes (2x A100-equivalent reserved for Redwood optimized runtime) + support
  - Annual seat/license + infra floor: $120k/year (covers reserved nodes + runtime license across envs)
  - Estimated blended unit: ~$900–$1,500 per 1M tokens (depends heavily on request size and KV cache hit rates)
- Option B: Committed token throughput (20–50M/month)
  - Commitment tiers: 20M/mo -> ~$1,300 per 1M; 50M/mo -> ~$950 per 1M
  - Overage: 20% premium per 1M over the commit band

Support tiers (short):
- Standard: business hours email + 48h SLAs on severity 1; included in base license.
- Prime: 24/7 on-call, 4h P1 response, quarterly architecture reviews, included for Dedicated/Enterprise.
- Enterprise: Prime + named TPM, on-site reviews, extended retention and SOC/custom audit support.

Suggested billing structure for Acme (recommended starter):
- 12-month committed token plan @ 40M/mo blended -> target ~$1,050 / 1M tokens (annual prepay or monthly invoiced).
- Include Prod+Staging in pooled entitlement; dev sandbox non-metered.
- Prime support for first 12 months if you want the faster response SLA for initial rollout.

Attachments included: acme_onprem_pricing_v1.xlsx (line-item cost model) and sow_template_v2.pdf (SOW outline). Also adding a HubSpot deal link and a draft DocuSign for a term sheet once we land on numbers.

Proposed next steps

2) I’ll update the spreadsheet with two commit scenarios (20M and 50M) and a reserved-node option, and share a proposed term sheet.
3) Marissa to confirm discount bands and approval thresholds.

If that aligns, I’ll block time for Tue and send an updated cost model by EOD Monday.

Ben

Ben — nice framing. For ACME I suggest we aim for an initial ask that leaves room for a 10–18% commercial discount depending on term length. Playbook guidance:
- If they commit 12 months at >= 36M/mo blended, allow up to 12% discount and include Prime support.
- If they choose reserved-node (2-node) + prepay annual license, prioritize a 15–18% discount band in exchange for a longer term (24 months) and a small onboarding credit.

Connor — be prepared to recommend the minimal node footprint for their latency target and call out any networking egress that would materially change cost (we need that detail to sign off on the reserved-node economics).
